<Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez>: The Small Business Administration's (SBA) Women-Owned Small Business (WOSB) Contracting Program is designed to help the government recruit women-owned small businesses and economically disadvantaged women-owned small businesses (EDWOSBs) into the federal marketplace and level the playing field when they compete for contracts.
The data shows that women are starting and running small businesses at increasingly similar rates to their male counterparts but they are not participating in the federal market at the same rate. The number of companies in the economy are overwhelmingly small, and about 40 percent woman-owned, while in the federal marketplace, just over 28 percent are small, and less than five percent are confirmed to be woman-owned.\1\
\1\Nat'l Women's Bus. Council, NWBC 2024 Annual Report, 45 (Dec. 2024), https://www.nwbc.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/NWBC-2024- Annual-Report.pdf.
The federal government attempts to expand contracting opportunities for WOSBs in two main ways: (a) setting an overall goal of awarding 5% of federal contracting dollars to women-owned firms; and (b) using streamlined authorities to make it easier for federal agencies to contract with women-owned firms. These authorities allow contracting officers to set-aside a contract for exclusively WOSBs competition and to sole source contracts to a WOSB firm if certain conditions are met.
The SBA's Office of Government Contracting and Business Development certifies applicants seeking to enter the WOSB Program. Currently, a WOSB must be certified to be awarded a contract that is set-aside or sole sourced. But if a women-owned small business who self-certifies their WOSB status is awarded a contract by a federal agency through other methods, that federal agencies can count the value of that contract toward their 5% procurement goal.
In 1994 when Congress first established the goal, it recognized the obstacles that female entrepreneurs face competing in the federal market, stating in the committee report: ``Given the slow progress to date . . . this goal may take some time to be reached.'' Three decades later, this remains an understatement.
The federal government topline goal of 5% for WOSBs has only been met twice and federal agencies routinely miss their individual WOSB goals, while the contracting authorities are underutilized and represent a tiny percentage of contracts that count towards the goal. Less than $2 billon of the almost $31 billion in contracts awarded to women-owned small businesses are solicited in a way that only WOSBs can compete.
While women-owned firms are not seeing the contracting opportunities that should accompany their level of participation in the market, the goals continue to have value. In addition to the government-wide goal, there are two other that are important for women-owned firms.
First, each federal agency attempts to meet their own 5% goal. This helps WOSBs with products or services unique to that agency's mission compete for their first government contract. In order to a federal agency, the company has likely met most of the government's unique requirements and can then more easily sell their products to other agencies. This process assists in expanding their markets and diversifying their customer base.
Second, large prime contractors have to meet subcontracting goals. There are challenges associated with subcontracting, subcontracting requirements, and data but for many small businesses, subcontracting is how they get a foot in the door to the federal marketplace.
The purpose of this legislation is to protect the integrity of the WOSB program and the WOSB goals but it will concurrently act as an incentive for more women-owned small businesses to get certified. This would allow agency personal to better and more frequently utilize the authorities designed to make contracting with WOSBs easier--bringing more opportunities to all WOSB firms and encouraging more women-owned small businesses to compete for government contracts.
Study after study shows a shrinking industrial base. The government has over 40% fewer small businesses in its ecosystem than a decade ago.\2\ More small businesses are leaving the federal market quicker and fewer and fewer are signing up to take their place. This exodus has disproportionately impacted women-owned firms: ``From FY20 to FY21, there was a 6 percent decline in small business owners awarded federal contracts, and WOSBs accounted for a quarter of that decline.''\3\
\2\Gov't Accountability Off., Small Business Contracting: Actions Needed to Implement and Monitor DoD's Small Business Strategy (Oct. 2021).
\3\Nat'l Women's Bus. Council, NWBC 2023 Annual Report, 47 (Dec. 2023), https://www.nwbc.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/ NWBC_AR_2023_FINAL-508.pdf.
Expanding and protecting the WOSB program, as this bill will do, will allow agencies to better utilize and leverage it to bring more new small businesses--and their talent, innovation, and solutions--into the federal marketplace.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Ranking Member.
